title: New to the world of coding and UE5 Blueprints. Is AI a tool for me? If so, which one?
author: Pretend-Educator7716
selftext: Hello all! I am trying to teach myself Blueprints for game dev. I have bought a few Udemy courses and gone through them and that's all well and good. The obvious issues arise when i try to go off on my own and implement anything new, I have no knowledge base to work off of and cannot work with Blueprints well enough to make the changes I desire. This leads me to searching all over the internet for hyper specific questions and getting no answers. Then, I turn to ChatGPT and try to ask it the same questions and it responds with information that sounds right but I still do no know how to implement the ideas. Is there a ( hopefully free/cheap) AI that is somewhat helpful in assisting folks like me get on the right path or is it still too early for AI to help with those that cannot distinguish between good suggestions and bad? If it isn't for me, what would you suggest is the best course for learning Blueprints and not be in tutorial hell? Thank you all!

comments.author: moneydollarz
comments.body:
AI Tools That Actually Help With Blueprints

Not all AI tools are created equal, especially when it comes to Unreal Engine. These are the ones I’ve found genuinely useful, especially if you’re trying to move from “watching” to “doing”:

Game Builder by LordVile
If you’re working in Unreal, this one’s a gem. It understands Blueprint logic and rendering systems, so you can ask it implementation-level questions like “Why isn’t this trigger working?” without getting vague answers. And yep, it’s free.

GitHub Copilot
It doesn’t plug directly into Unreal, but it’s great for logic-heavy stuff in VS Code. You can write something like, make player jump` and it’ll suggest the code. Free for students, or $10/month otherwise. Super handy for understanding flow and syntax.

Inworld AI
This one’s more for character behavior and dialogue prototyping. It’s not Blueprint-specific, but if you’re building dynamic NPCs, it’s worth exploring.

Want more? There’s a solid roundup of free AI tools for game devs [A], and another list of 15 AI tools for games [B] if you feel like going deeper.

Escaping Tutorial Hell: Blueprint Learning That Actually Sticks

If you’re tired of watching endless videos and still feeling lost, here’s how to start building real understanding:

Unreal’s Free Learning Portal
Unreal Online Learning has legit free courses, not just fluff. I recommend Blueprints and Gameplay for Game Designers and Interactive Material Swaps Using Blueprints. They’re practical and well-paced.

Coursera’s Masterclass
The Unreal Engine 5 Blueprints Game Developer Masterclass is hands-on and includes assignments. It walks you through everything from variables to UI and event dispatchers.

Build Something Small
Pick a simple game idea, flashlight horror, basic puzzle, whatever excites you, and break it into systems: movement, interaction, UI. Then tackle each one individually. Ask AI or forums for help on specific pieces, not the whole game.

Learn to Debug
Blueprint debugging tools like Breakpoints, Watch Variables, and Print Strings are lifesavers. They don’t just tell you what’s broken, they help you understand why.

Final Tip: Ask Smarter Questions

When you’re using AI, the way you ask matters. Try framing things like:

• “How do I make a Blueprint that spawns an actor every 5 seconds?”
• “Can you walk me through setting up a Blueprint interface between two actors?”
• “What’s the difference between casting and using event dispatchers?”

comments.author: DreamNotDeferred
comments.body:
I'm coming from the same place as you, and now I have multiple game mechanics up and running and working together well. I ended up using Gemini 2.5 pro at https://aistudio.google.com/.

First I told it the overall idea for the game I was trying to make, and referenced other published games that were similar. Then, I worked on one mechanic at a time, getting them working and then starting the next one. You tell it what you want to do, it provides steps on how to do it. Sometimes the steps assume you have certain knowledge, so ask more questions if needed, and it's good to tell Gemini at the beginning to explain every detail of every step to you, assuming you know nothing.

In case you don't know this, text AIs, called LLMs (large language models) work by converting the text you put in the chat into "tokens", and they place a limit on how many tokens you can use in a given time period. Google AI Studio allows you to have a limit of 1 million tokens with Gemini (a type of LLM), so you have time before hitting the limit.

FYI, though, Gemini will start to "hallucinate" (get things wrong) the higher the token count is, so what I've done is, when I get around the 100k-150k token mark, I'll ask it to generate a "Project So Far" document that details everything in the game, narratively, conceptually, and logic wise. Then I'll just start a new chat with Gemini, give it the document, and continue from there.

Give it a try and see what you think.

replies.author: Pretend-Educator7716
replies.body: Wow this is super interesting thank you very much! Glad it has been working out for you I will investigate it for sure!

replies.author: DreamNotDeferred
replies.body:
Yeah it has been working out well. I'm still at it. I have something that could very loosely be called "gameplay" lol, but game dev is a marathon, not a sprint. I forgot to mention, tell Gemini which unreal version you're using, and use the "zip projects" feature in Unreal to save versions of your project. Sometimes, the LLM will get things wrong, and take you down a rabbit hole of worse and worse advice, and it may take a while for you to figure out that you need to try a different approach for what you want to do; having a separate saved project from before you did all that saves you the headache of having undo the last several changes.

  
Give it a try, though. It's definitely not perfect, but if I can make progress, then anyone can.
